lead: Gas sensors turn the amount of a gas into a resistance, a current or a voltage. Three families cover most industrial needs. Oxygen is measured by the Nernst voltage of a hot zirconia cell, by the magnetic pull on oxygen molecules, or by a limiting current. Hydrogen is measured by palladium films and gates, by catalytic beads, or by thermal conductivity. Gas-sensitive resistors use a heated tin dioxide film whose resistance falls when a reducing gas arrives. They sit in kitchen LPG alarms, car exhausts, boilers and steel plants.
prereq: You need sensitivity and transfer functions from the static characteristics of sensors, and the Wheatstone bridge from resistive transducers. The full zirconia theory is in solid electrolyte and SAW sensors.

blocks.text: A zirconia cell is a tube or disc of ZrO₂ stabilised with yttria. It conducts O²⁻ ions usefully only above about 350 °C, so practical cells are heated to about 600 to 800 °C. Two porous platinum electrodes coat it: one sees reference air at 20.9 % oxygen, the other sees the sample gas. The cell gives a Nernst EMF:

blocks.where: E is the cell EMF in volts; R = 8.314 J/(mol·K); T is temperature in kelvin; F = 96 485 C/mol; p₁ is the oxygen partial pressure at the reference electrode and p₂ at the sample electrode; the 4 is the number of electrons in O₂ + 4e⁻ → 2O²⁻.

blocks.text: The output is logarithmic, so a small voltage covers a wide range. At 973 K (700 °C), a pressure ratio of 10 gives only about 48 mV. The reference side is positive when the sample is oxygen-poor. Car engine management, boiler flue gas and steel making use this cell. Full solid-electrolyte theory is in solid electrolyte and SAW sensors.

Paramagnetic oxygen sensors use the fact that O₂ has two unpaired electrons and is strongly paramagnetic; most other gases are weakly diamagnetic. A small glass dumb-bell or a heated wire sits in a magnetic field. Oxygen pulled into the field deflects the dumb-bell, or changes the pressure, and the deflection is read optically or capacitively. This gives a linear reading of percent-level oxygen and is common in flue-gas analysers.

An electrochemical limiting-current cell uses a zirconia disc with a tiny diffusion hole. A voltage is applied; all oxygen reaching the cathode is pumped, and the current saturates at a value set by diffusion. That saturation current is proportional to oxygen concentration, not logarithmic, which suits wide-range and automotive use.

In medicine, oxygen is measured on both sides of the patient. A fast paramagnetic analyser in an anaesthesia machine or ventilator reads the inspired and expired oxygen breath by breath. In blood, the Clark electrode measures the oxygen partial pressure pO₂: a platinum cathode held at about −0.6 to −0.7 V against an Ag/AgCl anode sits behind a thin oxygen-permeable membrane, every oxygen molecule that diffuses through is reduced (O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻), and the current is proportional to pO₂. It is the oxygen channel of every blood-gas analyser and the same electrode that sits under the first glucose biosensors.

Palladium absorbs hydrogen readily. A thin Pd film changes resistance when H₂ is absorbed; a Pd gate on a MOSFET changes the work function at the Pd/SiO₂ interface and shifts the flat-band voltage; a Pd/n-Si Schottky diode shows a drop in barrier height. These devices work near 100 °C or lower and can detect ppm levels, but they are slow to recover and are poisoned by sulphur compounds.

A catalytic pellistor has two alumina beads, each with a platinum wire coil. One bead carries a catalyst (platinum or palladium), the other is inert. Both are heated to about 500 °C. A combustible gas burns on the active bead and releases heat; the bead temperature rises, the Pt coil resistance rises, and a Wheatstone bridge unbalances. The bridge output is proportional to the heat of combustion, so it reads in % LEL. Oxygen must be present; silicones and lead poison the catalyst.

A thermal conductivity cell uses a heated wire in a small chamber. Hydrogen conducts heat about seven times better than air, so the wire loses heat faster and its resistance drops. This is cheap and robust for high hydrogen concentrations, but it is cross-sensitive to helium and carbon dioxide.

A gas-sensitive resistor, also called a chemiresistor, is a sintered bead or thick film of tin dioxide (SnO₂), often doped with a little palladium or platinum, on a ceramic tube. A heater coil inside holds it at 300–400 °C. In clean air, oxygen adsorbs on the surface as O⁻ and O²⁻, trapping conduction electrons, so the film has a high resistance. A reducing gas such as CO, H₂, LPG, methane or ethanol reacts with the adsorbed oxygen and returns electrons to the film, so the resistance falls.

blocks.where: S is the sensitivity (a ratio, no units); R<sub>air</sub> is the film resistance in clean air in ohms; R<sub>gas</sub> is the resistance in the test gas in ohms.

blocks.text: The heater is essential: at room temperature the surface reaction is too slow, and each gas has a temperature at which the response peaks. Selectivity is improved by dopants, by a filter layer, and by choosing the operating temperature. These sensors are cheap and sensitive but not selective; a kitchen alarm responds to cooking alcohol as well as LPG. Trade names include Taguchi. Sulphur gases such as H₂S are also sensed by SnO₂ films, using the same resistance-fall mechanism.

Semiconductor junction devices use a Pd/n-Si Schottky diode or a Pd-gate MOS capacitor. Hydrogen at the interface changes the barrier height or the flat-band voltage, which is read as a voltage shift. They are compatible with silicon processing and are used in low-power hydrogen leak detectors.

figure.caption: The cell at 973 K: oxygen is reduced to O²⁻ on the air side, the ions cross the hot zirconia and give up their electrons on the flue side. The EMF is (RT/4F) ln(20.9/2.0) = 20.96 mV × 2.347 = 49.2 mV, with the reference air electrode positive.

examples.question: A heated zirconia oxygen sensor sits in a boiler flue at 700 °C. Reference air is 20.9 % O₂ and the flue gas is 2.0 % O₂. Find the cell EMF and state which electrode is positive.
steps: Convert the temperature: T = 700 + 273 = 973 K. The Nernst equation always needs kelvin.
Write the Nernst equation: E = (RT/4F) ln(p₁/p₂), with p₁/p₂ = 20.9/2.0 = 10.45.
The reference air side has more oxygen, so the reference electrode is positive.
examples.answer: E = 49.2 mV, with the reference air electrode positive.
examples.check:
import math
R = 8.314
T = 973
F = 96485
ratio = 20.9 / 2.0
k = R * T / (4 * F) * 1000
print(round(k, 2))
print(round(math.log(ratio), 3))
print(round(k * math.log(ratio), 1))

traps: Using log₁₀ instead of ln in the Nernst equation. For a ratio of 10.45 at 973 K, log₁₀ gives 1.019 and an EMF of 21.4 mV instead of 49.2 mV.
Putting the temperature in degrees Celsius. At 700 °C, T = 973 K; using 700 in the formula gives 35.4 mV instead of 49.2 mV.
Dropping the 4 in 4F for the four-electron oxygen reaction. That makes the EMF four times too large.
Reversing the sign: the electrode with more oxygen is positive, so the reference air electrode is positive when the exhaust is oxygen-poor.
Thinking a chemiresistor's resistance rises for a reducing gas. It falls, because the gas returns trapped electrons to the SnO₂ film.
Confusing paramagnetic oxygen sensing with thermal-conductivity hydrogen sensing. Both are physical methods, but they exploit different properties and different gases.

quiz.q: What is the sensing material in a Taguchi gas sensor, and why is a heater needed?
quiz.a: Sintered or thick-film tin dioxide (SnO₂). The heater holds it at 300–400 °C so that oxygen adsorbs on the surface and the gas reaction is fast enough to give a usable resistance change.

quiz.q: Why does the zirconia cell EMF depend on the logarithm of the oxygen pressure ratio rather than linearly?
quiz.a: The cell is an electrochemical equilibrium: the Nernst equation relates EMF to the chemical potential difference, which contains ln(activity). A pressure ratio appears inside the logarithm, so equal ratios give equal voltage steps.

quiz.q: A SnO₂ sensor reads 60 kΩ in clean air and 4 kΩ in a gas sample. Find its sensitivity S.
quiz.a: S = R<sub>air</sub> / R<sub>gas</sub> = 60 kΩ / 4 kΩ = 15. It is a dimensionless ratio.

quiz.q: A zirconia cell at 800 °C has reference air at 20.9 % O₂ and sample gas at 1.0 % O₂. Find the EMF.
A pellistor shows no reading in a gas stream known to contain 2 % methane. Give two possible reasons.
quiz.a: No oxygen is present, so combustion cannot occur. The catalyst may be poisoned by silicones or lead. The heater may be open, or the bead may be cracked. Any two valid reasons with a short explanation.

quiz.q: Why does a Pd-gate MOSFET respond to H₂ but not to N₂?
quiz.a: Hydrogen dissociates on palladium and diffuses to the Pd/SiO₂ interface, changing the interface charge and the flat-band voltage. Nitrogen does not dissociate or absorb in Pd in the same way, so the gate voltage does not shift.

quiz.q: Distinguish a Nernst-mode zirconia oxygen sensor from a limiting-current oxygen sensor.
quiz.a: The Nernst cell gives an open-circuit EMF proportional to ln(p₁/p₂), which is logarithmic and needs a reference gas. The limiting-current cell applies a voltage and measures a saturation current set by diffusion through a small hole; that current is linear in oxygen concentration.

beyond: Not for the exam. Micro-hotplate SnO₂ films on silicon use a few tens of milliwatts and sit in arrays for electronic noses. Palladium alloys and optical fibres are used for hydrogen leak detection in fuel-cell vehicles. Tunable diode laser absorption measures ppm gases on a single spectral line. Photoacoustic and electrochemical micro-cells are moving into wearable air-quality monitors. Search for MEMS metal-oxide gas sensors, lambda sensors, pellistors and electronic noses.
